items.title: [ANN] odf v0.1.0: Pure-Crystal OASIS ODF 1.3 .ods reader and writer, zero dependencies
items.author: renich
items.content:
I just tagged , a pure-Crystal OASIS OpenDocument Format 1.3 shard built strictly on Crystal’s standard library (, , ) with zero runtime dependencies and zero C wrappers.

I needed self-contained static binaries that could generate and parse real spreadsheets with live formulas and proper styling without shelling out to Python or LibreOffice, so I built from the ground up.

  • Writer (Odf::Spreadsheet::Workbook): Multi-sheet workbooks, typed cells (, , , , , , , ), live OpenFormula expressions, cell merges, frozen panes, autofilters, and reusable styles/number formats.
  • Hardened Reader (): XXE-safe XML parsing, streaming Zip-bomb byte quotas, and bounded repeat-cell expansion.
  • Extensible Core (): and are document-agnostic, so adding , , and support does not require touching the container engine.
require "odf"

workbook = Odf::Spreadsheet::Workbook.new do |book|
  book.currency_style("usd", symbol: "$", decimals: 2, negative_red: true)

  book.sheet("BOM") do |sheet|
    sheet.freeze(rows: 1)
    sheet.header_row(["Qty", "Item", "Unit Price", "Total"])

    sheet.row do |row|
      row.integer(4)
      row.text("NVMe OSD Node")
      row.currency(12_500.00, style: "usd")
      row.formula("=[.A2]*[.C2]", cached: 50_000.00, style: "usd")
    end
  end
end

workbook.save("bom.ods")

doc = Odf::Spreadsheet::Reader.open("bom.ods")
puts doc.sheet("BOM")[1][3].as_f # => 50000.0

If anyone is interested in tackling , , or modules on top of , contributions and feedback are very welcome!

items.title: Disk View – a very small GTK4 desktop app and project blueprint
items.author: magynhard
items.content:
I’d like to share a little side project I’ve been working on: Disk View.

It’s a pretty simple Linux desktop app that shows all your drives, partitions, and their disk usage in one compact overview.

I wasn’t really happy with GNOME’s default Disks app when all I wanted was a quick overview of how much space was used across my drives. So I ended up building my own little tool. Nothing particularly fancy, but it does exactly what I was looking for.

The app is written in Crystal using GTK4 and libadwaita.

What might actually be more interesting to the Crystal community than the app itself is the project setup. It could serve as a starting point or reference for anyone interested in building native GTK4 desktop applications with Crystal. Especially the GitHub workflow and setup for AppImage and Flatpak.

  • GTK4/libadwaita integration using Crystal bindings

  • A fairly typical GNOME desktop app structure

  • Translations for multiple languages

  • A GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds AppImage and Flatpak packages and attaches them to GitHub releases

The project was AI-agent-engineered and took only a few days, as i already had ported another experimental project, that i originally wrote with Ruby and GTK4. But after it was running well, it did not do well on other systems … this was one of my main reasons to finally spend more time and interest on Crystal. But the original problem that brought me to Crystal was another NodeJS (CLI) project, that i will port soon to crystal, after i have released a stable release of my Crystal Language Plugin for Jetbrains IDEs.

A big thanks to Hugo Parente Lima (@hugopl) for his work on the GTK4 bindings and GI-Crystal. Without projects like these, building native GTK applications in Crystal would be a lot harder. Really appreciate the effort!

Anyway, I thought I’d share it here in case someone finds either the app or parts of its implementation useful.

Feedback is always welcome!

items.title: Athena 0.23.0 | Now with an ORM and proper sub-command support!
items.author: Blacksmoke16
items.content:
The major highlight of this release is the initial release of the component! It’s been a long time coming, and now ships with migrations and testing utilities. The other big theme is modularity: Athena is now the closest its ever been in its goal of having an ecosystem of independent, and reusable components. Athena Framework made many of the components that used to be required, optional. Each component is also more aware of what components are currently installed and are generally wired up/integrated automatically when required.

  • Initial release of , including database migrations and testing utilities
  • The , , , , and components are now optional within the component, with each component shipping its own bundle
  • Console-only applications without the framework, still with DI-powered commands
  • Improved sub-command support in the component, e.g. ./console docker compose up
  • The component now speaks version 1.0 of the Mercure protocol
  • Opt out of linking , OpenSSL, and zlib via compile time flags

Alongside the last release I shared an alpha of the Athena ORM to start gathering feedback. I’m pleased to say it’s now released as !

As a quick recap of what makes it different from the other ORMs in Crystal land:

  • No custom DSL, entities are normal Crystal classes that use annotations to map properties to columns, primary keys, and relationships
  • Data Mapper instead of ActiveRecord, entities know nothing about the database, and are instead managed by an
  • A Unit of Work tracks changes to entities and writes them all in a single transaction when flushed. Only changed values are included in an
  • An Identity Map ensures each row is only ever represented by one object
  • Native relationships, with collections lazily loaded the first time they’re used
require "athena-orm"
require "pg"

@[AORMA::Entity]
@[AORMA::Table(name: "posts")]
class Post < AORM::Entity
  @[AORMA::Column]
  @[AORMA::ID]
  @[AORMA::GeneratedValue]
  property! id : Int64

  @[AORMA::Column]
  property! title : String
end

ORM = AORM::EntityManagerFactory.new DB.open ENV["DATABASE_URL"]

ORM.with_entity_manager do |em|
  post = Post.new
  post.title = "Hello World"

  em.persist post
  em.flush # => INSERT INTO posts (title) VALUES (?)

  post.title = "Hello Athena"
  em.flush # => UPDATE posts SET title = ? WHERE id = ?

  em.find(Post, post.id).same? post # => true
  em.repository(Post).find_one_by title: "Hello Athena"
end

PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, and SQLite are supported out of the box, using the standard crystal-db driver shards. More could be added in the future, but I think this covers the more populare/common ones.

The ORM component of course works best when used within the framework/ecosystem, but can be used outside of it, even within other frameworks; mainly via the method in the earlier example. An example usage within the Athena ecosystem would be something along the lines of:

require "athena"
require "athena-orm/bundle" # This implicitly requires `athena-dependency_injection`

ADI.configure({
  orm: {
    url: ENV["DATABASE_URL"],
  },
})

@[ADI::Register]
class PostController < ATH::Controller
  def initialize(@em : AORM::EntityManagerInterface); end

  @[ARTA::Get("/post/{id}")]
  def post(id : Int64) : Post?
    @em.find Post, id
  end
end

It is worth calling out that “within the framework” really just means any shard using athena-dependency_injection for things to be wired up, the entire component.

Database migrations are opt-in via require "athena-orm/migrations", and are managed via console commands when the console component is installed and its bundle is registered. Each migration is a Crystal type that adds the SQL to apply its change in , and the SQL to revert it in :

class App::Migrations::Version20261014120000 < AORM::Migrations::AbstractMigration
  def description : String
    "Create the posts table"
  end

  def up : Nil
    self.add_sql "CREATE TABLE posts (id BIGSERIAL NOT NULL, title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id))"
  end

  def down : Nil
    self.add_sql "DROP TABLE posts"
  end
end

generates a blank migration, executes the ones that haven’t been executed yet, and / show where things stand. Being Crystal types, migrations can also contain logic, such as skipping a migration on a specific platform, or migrating data. See the Database Migrations guide for more information.

The ORM also comes with helpers that run each test in a database transaction that is rolled back once the test is done, so tests don’t see each other’s data. Within the framework, include AORM::Spec::DatabaseTransaction into an . Its is the same entity manager the container injects, so the requests made by the test run within the same transaction:

require "athena-orm/spec"

# Execute any pending migrations before the specs run
Spec.before_suite do
  AORM::Spec.migrate_database
end

struct PostControllerTest < ATH::Spec::APITestCase
  include AORM::Spec::DatabaseTransaction

  def test_show : Nil
    post = Post.new
    post.title = "Hello World"

    self.em.persist post
    self.em.flush

    self.get("/post/#{post.id}").body.should contain "Hello World"
  end
end

Applications using an AORM::EntityManagerFactory directly can inherit from instead.

Bundles went thru a re-think. The introduced last release, has been merged into the component itself as an optional opt-in entrypoint. Additionally, components are now more aware of what other components are installed. E.g. the component no longer requires the component directly, but must be installed in order to validate the dimensions of images. Compile time errors are raised where possible, but some runtime exceptions could not be avoided.

The idea of making almost every component optional was touched on in the last release. This release essentially accomplished that goal! An Athena Framework application no longer comes bundled with the , , , , and components. This ultimately results in smaller binaries that are faster to compile due to there being less extra code you don’t need.

The component based bundle approach used by the component was also expanded to many of the other components. This is the primary mechanism used to integrate the optional components into the framework. First add the ones you want to your and require them:

require "athena"

# Only require what the application needs
require "athena-serializer/bundle"
require "athena-validator/bundle"
require "athena-console/bundle"
require "athena-orm/bundle"
require "athena-mercure/bundle"
require "athena-clock"
require "athena-negotiation"

See the Optional Components section of the getting started guide for the full list. This change is of course breaking, but as usual, reference each component’s for more detailed migration instructions.

Console-only Applications

A nice side effect of this work is that the Dependency Injection component itself now registers the and services, along with any listeners, when those components are installed. Combined with the new console bundle, this means a console application gets the same DI-powered, lazily instantiated commands as it would within the framework, without having to require the framework, and with it, routing, the HTTP stack, etc:

require "athena-dependency_injection"
require "athena-console/bundle"

@[ADI::Register]
@[ACONA::AsCommand("app:create-user", description: "Creates a user")]
class CreateUserCommand < ACON::Command
  def initialize(@user_repository : UserRepository)
    super()
  end

  protected def execute(input : ACON::Input::Interface, output : ACON::Output::Interface) : ACON::Command::Status
    # ...

    Status::SUCCESS
  end
end

ACON::Application.new("My App", "1.0.0", ADI.container).run

On the same theme, this release also does a pass on the system libraries a framework application links against. A web framework needs Crystal’s HTTP stack, and with it OpenSSL and zlib, but applications that don’t need some of them can now opt out at build time:

  • - MIME types are only guessed based on file extensions
  • - cannot serve HTTPS, such as when TLS is terminated by a reverse proxy
  • - Crystal’s gzip/deflate support is unavailable

An application built with all three only links PCRE2 and the C runtime libraries Crystal always requires. See the System Dependencies section of the getting started guide for more information.

Commands that are namespaced, such as , may now be invoked as ./console docker compose up, with each level parsing its own options:

# `docker` parses `--context`, `docker:compose` parses `-f`, and `docker:compose:up` parses `web`
./console docker --context=prod compose -f app.yaml up web

The new command type can be used for a level that only groups other commands, listing its sub-commands when invoked without one. The running command can also read the options of its ancestors via ACON::Application#command_chain. See the API Docs for more information.

The Mercure protocol had its 1.0 release a while ago, which included quite a few breaking changes. The Mercure component, and its bundle, now speak it by default. Most notably the JWTs are now RFC 9068 access tokens built from , and the default authorization cookie name is now __Secure-mercure_access_token.

Hubs older than 1.0 can keep using the previous version of the protocol:

mercure: {
  hubs: {
    default: {
      url:              ENV["MERCURE_URL"],
      protocol_version: "0.x",
      jwt:              {
        secret: ENV["MERCURE_JWT_SECRET"],
      },
    },
  },
},

This release also fixes non-default hubs being removed from the hub registry, and only the last hub’s token aliases being registered, when configuring multiple hubs via the bundle. See the Mercure for more detailed instructions.

  • Event listeners typed with a generic event, such as , are now invoked for events of all descendants of the generic type, e.g. and
  • ADI::Spec::ContainerTestCase for testing services that require a container, and an annotation can now replace an alias defined by a bundle
  • The assertions accept a parameter to compile the code with compile time flags

At this point Athena has quite a few components that can be used in a wide range of contexts. However it is still missing some pretty core things as well; the main one being security related abstractions/features. As such, the next area of focus is going to be introducing some of the foundational parts of this that allow users to implement robust authorization and authentication logic without having to roll it themselves. I have some good plans for the design/implementation of this, but would love some feedback if anyone wants to share their specific use cases.

That’s it for this update! As usual, feel free to join me in the Athena Discord server if you have any suggestions, questions, ideas, or just want to chat!

items.title: CrymbleUI apps now run in the browser (WebAssembly)
items.author: wolfgang371
items.content:
Any CrymbleUI app now also builds, unchanged, as a static web page - the same Crystal compiled to WebAssembly, drawing on an HTML canvas. No server, nothing to install, it runs in the browser tab only.

Try it (desktop browser with mouse and keyboard; tested in Chromium and Firefox):

  • - a small app with CrymbleUI as a plain shard dependency (source) - the one to copy for your own app
  • - the full desktop data application, ~14k LOC, built from the same source as its Linux and Windows binaries
  • no in the app - the flavour is a property of the build: a second CrymbleUI backend paints the same pixels as the SFML one (checked against the desktop by a conformance suite)
  • puts into your app; then
    bin/crymble-web setup     # once: the toolchain (a few minutes, ~1 GB)
bin/crymble-web build     # bin/web/<target>/ - copy it to any static web server
bin/crymble-web serve     # try it locally
  • toolchain: Crystal 1.22.0 + a small compiler patch, wasi-sdk 25, Boehm GC 8.2.8, Binaryen - all pinned and built reproducibly by
  • the patch (in , every change explained in its header): wasm exceptions (stock 1.22 exits on ), struct returns from C, Boehm as the wasm32 collector (stock: no collection at all), and a few WASI file-system fixes - maybe of interest upstream?

Limits as of now: Safari not tried yet; the browser keeps some shortcuts for itself (Ctrl+W/N/T/Tab); files saved live in the tab only.

Versions: CrymbleUI v1.9.4 (src ~42k LOC, spec ~88k LOC - still fully AI generated), Embrace v2.6.1.

Feedback welcome - especially how it behaves in Safari and on a Mac!

items.title: Gcry 0.35.0: Crystal's own GC, written in pure Crystal, now runs the Crystal compiler itself
items.author: sdogruyol
items.content:
gcry is a garbage collector for Crystal, written entirely in Crystal. Zero C code, replaces Boehm with .

  • Speaks Boehm’s GC_* C ABI, so , spec/std (18,054 examples) and the compiler itself run on gcry as the process GC

  • Parallel mark on by default, marking 31% faster on x86-64, 37% on arm64

  • Two mark workers gained 8-16 points of Boehm’s speed on every GC-heavy workload

  • 48 fixes on the default path, root-complete defaults

The goal: Crystal’s own GC, no Boehm dependency. Getting closer every release.

items.title: Optimal Mersenne Primes Search Using Modular Groups
items.author: jzakiya
items.content:
I just released this paper (extracted from a larger journal article slated for Dec 2026) which uses Crystal code to show how to sequentially generate Mersenne Primes without computing 2^p - 1.

The code is the single core version. I haven’t had a chance yet to do the multi-core parallel version.

As these numbers become humongously large, it would require special software to generate and check 100s of digits values.

It would be nice if there could be some Crystal hooks into such existing software, to be able to write and run complete MPGS searches with it. So if anyone knows how to do that, or feels inspired to try, let me know.

items.title: Generic class new doesn't infer type var for instance var
items.author: 2f1cafc
items.content:
When is defined like this:

class Foo(T)
def initialize(@value : T); end
end

the following works fine as a local var, which matches the description in the Generics section of the spec:

x = Foo.new("hello") # Foo(String).new inferred

However when is an instance variable, it doesn’t work:

class Bar
@x = Foo.new("hello") # compile error: cannot infer type of @x
end

Instead I have to write @x = Foo(String).new("hello") . Is this a bug?

items.title: Accessing Google APIs via Crystal
items.author: nbrandaleone
items.content:
I work with Google Cloud often, and typically use Ruby to interface with the APIs. Ruby is an official SDK of Google Cloud. However, I prefer these days to things in Crystal if possible (it is all about speed!). However, crystal is not an official SDK of Google.

Well, I was able to write a generator that creates crystal shards from the Google Discovery docs (similar to openSDK specs). This is similar to how almost all the official languages are generated these days. The most recent language (Rust) acknowledges this in the README.

At the moment, there is only one library generated (Cloud Storage), but I am working on generating all the SDKs. Of course, when I say I wrote the code, I really meant that I worked with an AI tool to create it. Thus, it is not idiomatic - but it works… :-)

items.title: Announcing krikri - An Ansible compatible engine written in Crystal
items.author: weirdbricks
items.content:
I absolutely love Ansible and wanted to see if I could get AI to rewrite it in Crystal and if it could make it faster.

It’s 2 times faster on cold runs than Ansible and about 7 times faster on warm runs. I also compared against Mitogen: 1.3 times faster on cold runs and about 3 times faster on warm runs.

I’ve tested it against thousands of existing Ansible roles from Ansible galaxy to ensure compatibility.

There’s obviously some things that krikri doesn’t support like all the custom Python plugins, inventory plugins and community modules.

items.title: Reaching out to maintainers of downstream Crystal packages
items.author: straight-shoota
items.content:
Thank you for helping to make Crystal available in downstream package repositories. It’s much appreciated.

I’m reaching out to the maintainers of Crystal packages because I’d like to start a conversation about how we could better connect and ask how we could improve the packaging workflow for Crystal. For example, sometimes we need to communicate changes that affect packaging in an upcoming release. We usually mention that in the release notes, and the release pre-announcement published on the Crystal forum.

As a current important notification, the upcoming release 1.22 requires requires 1.14 or higher as bootstrap compiler.

I believe it would be great to have a dedicated space for coordination and collaboration between upstream and downstream projects, as well as between downstreams from different ecosystems. Discussions about packaging are already happening in different places, such as the Crystal forum, random GitHub issues, and other channels. Having a dedicated space would improve exposure and accessibility.

Now the question is how would that look like? What communication tool would you prefer?

My preference would be a dedicated category in the Crystal forum. Most community members are already there, the infrastructure exists. Active participation requires a forum account, but you could passively read and subscribe to RSS feeds.

But I’m open for your suggestions. If you prefer an open mailing list, for example, we could consider that.

Maybe we can borrow established good practices from other communities, so I’m eager to learn about that.

I’m posting this topic in the forum as a starter, but I’m also reaching out directly to known maintainers of Crystal packages which do not have a forum account. I’ll forward any responses from those direct communications.

items.title: CodeGraph support for Crystal — feedback wanted
items.author: n-rodriguez
items.content:
It extracts modules, classes, structs, enums, lib/fun bindings, macros, accessor macros (getter/property…) and cross-file calls, inheritance and

mixins. It indexes the compiler repo (2,423 files) as well as kemal and lavinmq.

A/B on those three repos, 3 questions each, 2 runs per arm: wall-clock -46%, tool calls -65%, file reads -75%. Cost only -4%.

  • macros are not expanded, so macro-generated methods (Kemal’s/ DSL) have no symbol;
  • overloaded visitors () are where it falls back to grep: static extraction can’t tell which overload is reached.

The PR has been waiting for review since July. If you work on Crystal code with an agent, trying the branch and reporting on the PR would help it land.

Feedback on the extraction choices (macro expansion in particular) is welcome.

I’m not affiliated with CodeGraph or its author in any way, beyond having submitted this PR as an outside contributor. Nothing to sell here: I just

want to share what I’ve seen, because I think it can be useful to people

writing Crystal with an agent.

items.title: Milestone: Running an Offline Kemal App with DNF on Fedora Linux! 🎉
items.author: renich
items.content:
We wanted to share an exciting milestone from our work on the ():

Today, we successfully ran a Kemal web application inside a network-isolated container (), after installing Kemal directly as a system library with !

No , no network calls, no , no , no local directory, and no vendored tarballs. Just:

# dnf install crystal crystal-kemal

And in a single script ():

require "kemal"

get "/" do
  "Hello from Fedora Crystal (100% offline)!"
end

Kemal.run

Running immediately compiled, resolved all transitive dependencies (, , ), and served HTTP requests completely offline.

While Fedora’s packaging guidelines permit standalone leaf applications to vendor dependencies (similar to Go and Rust using a ), distributing reusable shard libraries as unbundled system packages has historically been a challenge. Distributing compiled binaries doesn’t work for Crystal because of compile-time macros, generics monomorphization, and whole-program optimizations.

We solved this through three simple mechanisms:

  1. : When building the Fedora compiler RPM, we injected /usr/share/crystal/shards into :
    CRYSTAL_PATH="lib:/usr/share/crystal/shards:/usr/share/crystal/src"
  2. : We package reusable shard libraries as uncompiled source trees into versioned directories (e.g. /usr/share/crystal/shards/kemal-1.14.0/). This leaves the full AST available to the compiler so macros, generics, and LLVM inlining work natively at build time.
  3. The LLVM Primary Symlink Model: To allow single scripts to do while still letting multiple library versions coexist on the system without RPM package collisions:
    • The primary package provides an unversioned symlink:/usr/share/crystal/shards/kemal -> kemal-1.14.0
    • Compatibility packages (like ) live in their own versioned directory without the unversioned symlink.
    • For complex projects with a , our companion tool reads the lockfile and creates local symlinks in pointing directly to system packages—again, completely offline, reproducible, and without touching Git state.

As a bonus during our verification, Crystal 1.21.1’s new concurrency model and multi-threaded fibers ran effortlessly in the same offline container. Resizing the default execution context or creating worker pools scaled smoothly across system threads:

Observed threads: DEFAULT-0, DEFAULT-1, DEFAULT-2, DEFAULT-3

Concurrent compute fibers executed in parallel across all worker threads with zero hitches.

What Does This Mean for the Ecosystem?

  1. True Air-Gapped Development: You can now develop Crystal applications in high-security, offline environments (finance, telecom, defense, offline laptops) using standard system packages without needing internet access or manual vendoring.
  2. First-Class Distro Shards: Reusable Crystal shard libraries can be installed and managed cleanly via distribution packages, receiving system security updates and CVE tracking.
  3. : Anyone can install a library with and immediately write a one-off script using without initializing a whole shard workspace.

Come Join the Fedora Crystal SIG!

We are actively building out the Crystal packaging ecosystem in Fedora and EPEL, testing compiler builds on Rawhide and Fedora 44+, and packaging key community shards.

If you love Crystal and want to help with packaging, testing, or shaping how Crystal integrates with Linux distributions, we would love to have you with us!

Cheers, & (AI pair programmer collaborating with Rénich)

items.title: Macro hook for full file
items.author: Jochen
items.content:
Ok, this one is probably going to be horrible, but hear me out. We are using Crystal a lot to create DSLs, and I wanted to put this out there and ask if other DSL authors would find this useful, too?

One of the DSLs should have the following structure:

require "horrible/dsl"

namespace Some::Namespace

# DSL Stuff goes here, all top level

We now need to wrap everything following in some blocks (module, class, whatever). So we would need a hook that calls the namespace macro with everything below it as a block. I guess right now, there’s no way to do this.

For added horribleness, there could be multiple namespaces, meaning each namespace macro would get as block the content up to the next namespace, or the end of the file.

Sorry for inducing any pain, but them’s the requirements…

items.title: Upcoming 1.22 release
items.author: straight-shoota
items.content:
The next Crystal release, is scheduled for .

As usual, it is precluded by a two-week feature , starting today (). We’re using this time to consolidate the changes and fix bugs.

  • Crystal processes exit immediately when writing to STDOUT or STDERR fails with . This closely resembles the default behaviour of the signal. You can opt out of this behaviour by setting STDOUT.exit_on_broken_pipe = false. (#17335)
  • Reduced forward compatibility: Building Crystal 1.22 requires a stage-0 compiler at 1.14 or higher (RFC 30).
  • Major refactor of DWARF loader, with significant performance improvements.
  • All targets support a native event loop now, the fallback is becoming obsolete.
  • Constants can have type declarations (#16951)
  • and (#17392)
  • Support for LLVM 23.1 and 24.0 (#17432)
  • OpenSSL Kernel TLS is enabled by default (#17059)
  • Lots of HTTP bug fixes and other bug fixes
  • Upgrades of package dependencies, docker base images etc.

Nightly builds reflect the upcoming stable release! Please test your code base against nightly builds and report any regressions

items.title: Py-crystal — write Python extension modules in Crystal`
items.author: ralsina
items.content:
First, a disclaimer. I have been the manager in this project, I don’t how it works. Several LLMs have spent a few hundred million tokens writing it :-)

So, I leave you to their announcement

is a framework for writing Python extension modules in Crystal: statically compiled, GC-managed, and expressive — with the ergonomics of PyO3 for Rust and nimpy for Nim. Crystal exceptions become typed Python exceptions, ownership across the two heaps is handled automatically, and the whole C-API plumbing layer is generated at compile time from a small DSL, in either an annotation style or a block style.

A taste — a word counter that Python can iterate, size, compare, and add:

require "pycr"

Pycr.pyclass WordCounter, "demo.WordCounter" do
  pynew def initialize
    @words = [] of String
  end

  pymethod def add(word : String) : Int32
    @words << word
    @words.size
  end

  pyiter def each : Iterator(String)   # for w in wc
    @words.each
  end

  pylen def size : Int32               # len(wc)
    @words.size
  end

  pyadd def plus(other : WordCounter) : WordCounter
    merged = WordCounter.new
    (@words + other.@words).each { |w| merged.add(w) }
    merged
  end
end

from demo import WordCounter

a, b = WordCounter(), WordCounter()
a.add("crystal"); a.add("python")
b.add("static")

assert len(a) == 2
assert [w for w in a] == ["crystal", "python"]
assert (a + b).size == 3
assert a > b                       # rich comparison on word count

class Loud(WordCounter):           # Python subclassing, super() included
    def add(self, word):
        return super().add(word.upper())

Everything is generated at compile time from those signatures: argument conversion with on mismatch, mapped to Python’s , iterators that survive GC cycles mid-stream. And the hard problems of hosting a second runtime inside CPython are solved and tested — foreign Python threads get full access to Crystal’s fiber scheduler through a custom execution context with the GIL released, Boehm’s collector coexists with CPython’s through a serialized collection policy, and ownership across the two heaps is handled by a pin registry plus owned references. The whole thing passes a stress gauntlet and ships as one binary validated against CPython 3.11 through 3.14.

It’s fast, with a real consumer to prove it: wraps the tartrazine highlighter in ~150 lines of DSL and benchmarks 11–12× faster than Pygments on real files (0.8 ms vs 9.1 ms at 300 lines) with , and ~0.1 ms of per-call overhead. The project is MIT-licensed at — a self-contained wheel (Linux x86_64, CPython 3.11–3.14) is on the v0.1.0 release, installable with pip install <that wheel URL>, with CI building and smoke-testing a fresh wheel on every push.
